¶
'''breathful†''' (breth′fụl), ''a.'' [< ''breath'' + ''-ful.''] '''1.''' Full of breath: as, “the ''breathfull'' bellowes,” ''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 38.—'''2.''' Odorous; fragrant.
{{smaller block|Fresh Costmarie and ''breathfull'' Camomill.
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 195.}}}}

'''breathing''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''brethynge'', a current of air; verbal n. of ''breathe'', ''v.''] '''1.''' Respiration; the act of inhaling and exhaling air: as, “a difficulty of ''breathing'',” ''Melmoth'', tr. of Pliny, vi. 16.
{{smaller block|<poem>She sleeps: her ''breathings'' are not heard
In palace chambers far apart. ''Tennyson'', Day-Dream.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Aspiration; secret prayer or desire.
{{smaller block|Earnest desires and ''breathings'' after that blessed state.
{{right|''Tillotson'', Sermons, I. xxiv.}}}}
'''3.''' Aërial motion; respiratory action.
{{smaller block|<poem>There’s not a ''breathing'' of the common wind
That will forget thee.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', To Toussaint l’Ouverture.}}}}
'''4.''' Figuratively, a gentle influence or operation; inspiration: as, the ''breathings'' of the Spirit.
{{smaller block|<poem>The air
Is like a ''breathing'' from a rarer world. ''N. P. Willis.''</poem>}}
'''5†.''' A breathing-place; a vent.
{{smaller block|<poem>The warmth distends the chinks, and makes
New ''breathings'', whence new nourishment she takes.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''6.''' Physical exercise, from the fact that it calls the lungs into free play: as, the Oxford crew took their ''breathings'' every morning at ten.
{{smaller block|I lack ''breathing'' and exercise of late. {{right|''Scott.''}}}}
'''7.''' Utterance; words.

{{smaller block|<poem>Swiche a fairenesse of a nekke
Had that swete that bone nor ''brekke''
Nas ther noon seen.</poem>

''Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''6.''' A field. [Suffolk, Eng.]

'''bred<sup>1</sup>''' (bred). Preterit and past participle of ''breed.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|breathe|673|breech}}</noinclude>To breathe one’s last'', to die.
{{smaller block|<poem>He, safe return’d, the race of glory past,
New to his friends’ embrace, had ''breath’d his last.''</poem>
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}

'''breathed''' (bretht), ''a.''   [< ''breath'', ''n.'', + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Endowed with breath; exercised.
{{smaller block|<poem>A man so ''breath’d'', that certain he would fight, yea,
From morn till night.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If I be just, all praises must
Be given to well-''breathed'' Jilian Thrust.</poem>
{{right|''Shirley'', Hyde Park, iv. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' Out of breath.
{{smaller block|Mr. Tulkinghorn arrives in his turret-room, a little ''breathed'' by the journey up. {{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, xli.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''philol.'', uttered with breath as distinguished from voice; surd or mute.—'''4.''' In compounds, having that capacity for breathing indicated by the prefix: as, ''short-breathed.''

'''breather''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who breathes or lives.
{{smaller block|<poem>She shows a body rather than a life;
A statue, than a ''breather.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' One who utters or whispers.
{{smaller block|<poem>For my authority bears of a credent bulk,
That no particular scandal once can touch,
But it confounds the ''breather.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 4.}}}}
'''3.''' One who animates or inspires.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''breather'' of all life does now expire;
His milder Father summons him away.</poem>
{{right|''Norris.''}}}}
'''4.''' Anything, as a walk, gymnastic exercise, etc., that stimulates or gives healthy action to the breathing organs. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|<poem>So here we are at last—that hill’s a ''breather.''</poem>
{{right|''Colman the Younger'', Poor Gentleman, iv. 11.}}}}

'''breathful†''' (breth′fụl), ''a.''   [< ''breath'' + ''-ful.'']   '''1.''' Full of breath: as, “the ''breathfull'' bellowes,” ''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 38.—'''2.''' Odorous; fragrant.
{{smaller block|Fresh Costmarie and ''breathfull'' Camomill.
{{right|''Spenser'', Muiopotmos, l. 195.}}}}

'''breathing''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brethynge'', a current of air; verbal n. of ''breathe'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' Respiration; the act of inhaling and exhaling air: as, “a difficulty of ''breathing'',” ''Melmoth'', tr. of Pliny, vi. 16.
{{smaller block|<poem>She sleeps: her ''breathings'' are not heard
In palace chambers far apart. ''Tennyson'', Day-Dream.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Aspiration; secret prayer or desire.
{{smaller block|Earnest desires and ''breathings'' after that blessed state.
{{right|''Tillotson'', Sermons, I. xxiv.}}}}
'''3.''' Aërial motion; respiratory action.
{{smaller block|<poem>There’s not a ''breathing'' of the common wind
That will forget thee.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', To Toussaint l’Ouverture.}}}}
'''4.''' Figuratively, a gentle influence or operation; inspiration: as, the ''breathings'' of the Spirit.
{{smaller block|<poem>The air
Is like a ''breathing'' from a rarer world. ''N. P. Willis.''</poem>}}
'''5†.''' A breathing-place; a vent.
{{smaller block|<poem>The warmth distends the chinks, and makes
New ''breathings'', whence new nourishment she takes.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''6.''' Physical exercise, from the fact that it calls the lungs into free play: as, the Oxford crew took their ''breathings'' every morning at ten.
{{smaller block|I lack ''breathing'' and exercise of late. {{right|''Scott.''}}}}
'''7.''' Utterance; words. {{smaller block|I am sorry to give ''breathing'' to my purpose.
{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., i. 3.}}}}
'''8.''' Time taken to recover breath; hence, a stop; a delay.
{{smaller block|Come, you shake the head at so long a ''breathing.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Give me a little ''breathing'', till I can
Be able to unfold what I have seen.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou hast open’d our difficult and sad times, and given us an unexpected ''breathing'' after our long oppressions.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}}}
'''9.''' In ''gram.'', aspiration or its absence, or a sign indicating it. {{smaller|In Greek there are two breathings—the aspirate (''spiritus asper'') or the rough breathing, indicated by a mark (‘) equivalent to our letter ''h'', and the lenis (''spiritus lenis'') or the smooth breathing (’), indicating simply the absence of the rough. Thus ὁς is equal to ''hos'', but ἰς to ''is''.—'''Breathing capacity.''' See ''capacity''.}}

'''breathing-hole''' (brē′ᴛʜing-hōl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A vent-hole, as in a cask.—'''2.''' One of the spiracles or stigmata through which insects respire. Also called ''breathing-pore''.—'''3.''' The spiracle or blow-hole of a cetacean.—'''4.''' A hole in the ice where an aquatic mammal, as a seal, comes up to breathe.

'''breathing-mark''' (brē′ᴛʜing-märk), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''music'', a small mark (*, ’, or √) placed above a vocal score, indicating the point at which the singer may properly take breath.—'''2.''' Same as ''spiritus''.

'''breathing-place''' (brē′ᴛʜing-plās), ''n.'' '''1.''' A place where fresh air can be breathed; a vent.
43 {{smaller block|Each bough . . . finding some sufficient ''breathing-place'' among the other branches.
{{right|''Ruskin'', Elem. of Drawing, p. 194.}}}}

'''2.''' The place for a pause in a sentence or a poetic verse; a cesura.

{{smaller block|That cæsura, or ''breathing-place.''
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Defence of Poesy.}}}}

'''breathing-pore''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing-pōr), ''n.'' '''1.''' In ''physiol.'', a microscopic aperture for the escape or admission of air, as in the cuticle of plants. See ''stoma.''—'''2.''' Same as ''breathing-hole'', 2.

'''breathing-space''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing-spās), ''n.'' A breathing-time; an intermission of exertion.

'''breathing-time''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing-tīm), ''n.'' Pause; relaxation.

{{smaller block|We may have some ''breathing-time'' between our promise and its accomplishment.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Cases of Conscience.}}}}

'''breathing-tube''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing-tūb), ''n.'' In ''entom.'', the respiratory tube of certain aquatic larvæ and dipterous puparia. {{smaller|It is a slender integumental prolongation, bearing at the tip one or both of the anal stigmata, through which the insect obtains air at the surface of the water or semifluid filth in which it lives. The breathing-tube is also possessed by certain adult heteropters.}}

'''breathing-while''' (brē′ᴛ̵ʜing-hwīl), ''n.'' An intermission of exertion; a breathing-time.   ''Shak.''

<poem>Except when for a ''breathing-while'' at eve,
Some niggard fraction of an hour, he ran
Beside the river-bank.   ''Tennyson'', Aylmer’s Field.</poem>

'''breathless''' (breth′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''brethles''; < ''breath'' + ''-less.'']   '''1.''' Without breath; dead.

<poem>Denies the rites of funeral fires to those
Whose ''breathless'' bodies yet he calls his foes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 84.}}}}

'''2.''' Out of breath; spent with labor or exertion. {{smaller block|<poem>Unwounded from the dreadful close,
But ''breathless'' all, Fitz-James arose.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., v. 16.}}}}
'''3.''' That takes away the breath.
{{smaller block|How I remember that ''breathless'' flight!
{{right|''Longfellow'', Golden Legend, iv.}}}}
'''4.''' Marked by an apparent forgetfulness to breathe; absorbed; eager; excited.
{{smaller block|The young folks would crowd around the hearth, listening with ''breathless'' attention to some old crone of a negro, who was the oracle of the family.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 168.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The holy time is quiet as a nun
''Breathless'' with adoration.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Misc. Sonnets, i. 30.}}}}

'''breathlessness''' (breth′les-nes), ''n.'' The state of being breathless or out of breath with exertion; difficulty in breathing.

'''breath-sound''' (breth′sound), ''n.'' In ''physiol.'', a sound caused by the movement of the air in the lungs in respiration. Also called ''respiratory murmur''.—{{smaller|'''Cogged breath-sound''', in ''pathol.'', an interrupted or jerky respiratory sound, most marked in inspiration. Also called ''cog-wheel respiration''.}}

'''breccia''' (brech′iä̤), ''n.''   [It., formerly also ''brecchia'', gravel, now technically breccia, = F. ''brèche'', connected with It. ''breccia'' = Sp. Pg. ''brecha'', < F. ''brèche'', a breach; all of Teut. origin: see ''breach'', and cf. ''brash''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   In ''geol.'', a conglomerate in which the fragments, instead of being rounded or water-worn, are angular. {{smaller|The term is most frequently applied to volcanic masses made up of fragments which have become consolidated into rock before becoming rounded by friction against each other or by the action of water.}}

[[File:century v01 p0699 c2f1.png|center|257px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Breccia.—Polished Surface.}}}}

'''brecciated''' (brech′i-ā-ted), ''a.''   [< ''breccia'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having the character of a breccia.
{{smaller block|According to Professor Ramsay the ''brecciated'', subangular conglomerates and boulder beds of the Old Red Sandstone . . . are of glacial origin.
{{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Time, p. 294.}}}}

'''brecciation''' (brech-i-ā′shọn), ''n.''   [< ''breccia'' + ''-ation.'']   The condition of being brecciated. See ''breccia''.

'''brecht†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''breech''.

'''brecham''' (breċh′am), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''brechame;'' prob. of Celtic origin: cf. Gael. ''braighdeach'', a horse’s collar, ''braighdean'', a cow’s or calf’s collar, = Ir. ''braighdean'', a collar, Gael. ''braidean'', a little collar, dim. of ''braid'', a horse-collar, a brecham, = Ir. ''braid'', a collar, < Gael. Ir. ''braghad'', neck, throat, windpipe.]   A collar for a work-horse. [Scotch.]

'''brechan, breckan''' (brek′a̤n), ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''bracken.''

'''breche<sup>1</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''breech.''

'''breche<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''breach.''

'''Brechites''' (bre-kī′tēz), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βρέχειν, to wet: see ''rain'', and cf. ''aspergillum.'']   Same as ''Aspergillum'', 2.

'''breck''' (brek), ''n.''   [< ME. ''brekke'', var. of ''breke'', a break, breach, etc.: see ''breach'', and cf. ''break'', ''n.'', ''brick''<sup>1</sup>, and ''brack''<sup>1</sup>, all ult. < ''break'', q. v.]   '''1†.''' A break; breach; fracture.   ''Tusser.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Swiche a fairenesse of a nekke
Had that swete that bone nor ''brekke''
Nas ther noon seen.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 940.}}}}
'''2†.''' A bruise.   ''Kersey'', 1708.—'''3†.''' A breach; a gap in a hedge.—'''4.''' [Also called ''break''; prop. land broken up and allowed to lie fallow.] A piece of uninclosed arable land; a sheepwalk, if in grass.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''5.''' A large new-made inclosure.   ''Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''6.''' A field. [Suffolk, Eng.]
{{smaller block|The bird’s chosen breeding-place was in wide fields—''brecks'', as they are locally called—of winter-corn.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IV. 578.}}}}

'''breckan''', ''n.'' See ''brechan.''

'''breckins''' (brek′inz), ''n.'' A dialectal variant of ''bracken.''

'''bred<sup>1</sup>''' (bred). Preterit and past participle of ''breed.''

'''bred'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''bread''<sup>1</sup>.

'''brede'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''bread''<sup>2</sup>.

'''brede'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''n.'' See ''bread''<sup>3</sup>, ''braid''<sup>1</sup>.

'''brede'''<sup>3</sup>†, ''v. t.''   [Early mod. E., < ME. ''breden'', < AS. ''brǣdan'', roast: see ''brawn''.]   To roast.

'''bredge'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''bridge''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bredge'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''v. t.'' See ''bridge''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bred-sore'''† (bred′sōr), ''n.'' A whitlow, or a sore coming without a wound or visible cause. Also called ''breeder''.

'''bree'''<sup>1</sup> (brē), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''brie'', ''brue'', ''broo'', < ME. ''bre'', full form ''brewe'', < AS. ''brīw'', also ''brīg'', a pottage of meal, pulse, etc., = Fries. ''bry'' = D. ''brij'' = MLG. ''brī'', ''brīg'' = OHG. ''brīo'', MHG. ''brī'', ''brīe'', G. ''brei'', broth, etc. Connection with ''brew''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' (AS. ''breówan'', etc.), is doubtful.]   Broth; soup; juice; sauce; water; moisture of any kind. [Scotch.]

'''bree'''<sup>2</sup> (brē), ''n.'' A dialectal variant of ''bray''<sup>4</sup>, ''brae''.

'''bree'''<sup>3</sup> (brē), ''v. t.''   [E. dial.]   To frighten.   ''Halliwell.'' [North. Eng.]

'''bree'''<sup>4</sup> (brē), ''n.'' A dialectal variant of ''brow''.

'''breech''' (brēch), ''n.''   [< ME. ''breech'', ''breche'', ''brech'', also unassibilated ''breke'', ''brek'', prop. pl. and meaning ‘breeches,’ the covering of the breech (whence the double pl. ''breeches'', the now prevalent form in that sense: see ''breeches''), < AS. ''brēc'', also ''brǣc'' (pl. of the unrecorded sing. *''brōc''), breeches (the additional sense of ‘breech,’ given by Bosworth, rests on a doubtful translation of a single passage), = OFries. ''brōk'', pl. ''brēk'', = D. ''broek'' = MLG. ''brōk'', LG. ''brook'' = OHG. bruoh'', MHG. ''bruoch'', G. ''bruch'' = Icel. ''brōk'', pl. ''brækr'', breeches (Sw. ''bracka'', breeches, ''brok'', naut., breeching), = ODan. ''brog'', breeches, hose, Dan. ''brog'', naut., breeching. Cf. L. ''brācæ'', pl., breeches (> It. ''braca'' = Sp. Pg. ''braga'' = Pr. ''braya'' = OF. ''braie'', breeches, F. ''braie'', a swaddling-band, > E. ''bray''<sup>5</sup> and ''brail'', q. v.), regarded as of Celtic origin; cf. Bret. ''bragez;'' but the Gael. Ir. ''brigis'', breeches, is perhaps from E. The relation of the Teut. forms to the Celtic is uncertain.]   '''1†.''' Breeches.
{{smaller block|Thyn olde ''breech.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Pardoner’s Tale, l. 486.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>That you might still have worn the petticoat,
And ne’er have stol’n the ''breech'' from Lancaster.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., v. 5.}}}}
'''2.''' The lower part of the body behind.—'''3.''' The hinder part of anything; specifically, the mass of metal behind the bore of a cannon, or the part of a small arm back of the barrel, including the rear of the latter in breech-loaders.—'''4.''' ''Naut.'', the angle of a knee-timber, the inside of which is called the ''throat''.

'''breech''' (brēch), ''v.''   [< ''breech'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To put into or clothe with breeches.
{{smaller block|Who was anxious to know whether the blacksmith’s youngest boy was ''breeched''. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xx.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Have I not shaved my people, and ''breeched'' them?</poem>
{{right|''Landor'', Peter the Great.}}}}
'''2.''' To cover to the breech or hilt. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>There, the murtherers,
Steep’d in the colours of their trade, their daggers
Unmannerly ''breech’d'' with gore.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Various other readings and interpretations, such as ''reech''ed''''}} (soiled with a dark yellow), ''drenched'', ''sheathed'', etc., have been proposed by Shaksperian commentators.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
